title: How to choose a treatment program
intro: Insurance tells you who will pay. It doesn't tell you who will help. Ask every program these questions, and walk away from the red flags.

ask.q: Are you licensed by the state and accredited by The Joint Commission or CARF? What's your license number?
ask.why: Check the number yourself on your state's licensing website.

ask.q: What level of care do you recommend for them, and why?
ask.why: A good program assesses first. Beware of one answer for everyone.

ask.q: Where does medical detox happen: on site, or somewhere else?
ask.why: Alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal need medical care.

ask.q: Do you offer or allow medication for addiction, such as buprenorphine, methadone, or naltrexone?
ask.why: For opioids, medication is one of the strongest protections against overdose.

ask.q: Do you treat depression, anxiety, trauma, and other mental health conditions at the same time?
ask.why: Most people in treatment need both, and treating one alone often fails.

ask.q: Who is on staff, and how often will they see a licensed counselor or therapist?
ask.why: Ask for names and licenses, not just job titles.

ask.q: What does your family program look like?
ask.why: Families who take part give their loved one a better chance.

ask.q: How do you decide when they're ready to leave, and what's the aftercare plan?
ask.why: Length of stay should follow progress, not the number of days insurance covers.

ask.q: What will it cost us after insurance? Can you put that in writing?
ask.why: Get the number before admission, not after.

flags: They offer free travel, free housing, cash, or gifts if your loved one comes.
"We take all insurance," or a promise that it will cost you nothing.
A hotline or "placement" service that won't tell you the facility's name, address, or license number.
Pressure to decide on this call, or to leave before you've seen the program.
They can't explain the treatment plan or the staff's credentials.
They suggest switching insurance plans or offer to pay the premiums. That's patient brokering, a federal crime and illegal in many states.
before: Look up the license on your state's website, and search the program's name with "complaints" or "lawsuit".
For more options, use FindTreatment.gov or call SAMHSA's free, confidential helpline at 1-800-662-4357.
Ask for the acceptance letter and the admission date in writing.
Have the bed, the date, and the ride ready before you ask them to say yes.
